text:
Short answer: no, it isn't a sign of anything on its own, and leading with it would hurt you.

**Why the panel composition is weak evidence**

A four-person panel being all one gender isn't unusual. In risk and compliance functions, and especially once you add HR representation to a hiring panel, women are often well represented — so an all-women panel of four can easily arise without any selection effect. You'd need to know the gender distribution of the relevant senior population at that bank to say whether four-for-four is even surprising, and you almost certainly don't.

More to the point, the research on same-gender panels is genuinely mixed. Several large studies of academic and public-sector hiring have found that female-majority panels are *not* more likely to select women, and a few found the opposite of what people assume. It's not a reliable inference in either direction.

**Why raising it would cost you**

If you put this in a letter, you've made an insinuation you can't support, and the conversation stops being about the substance of the decision. It also signals that your real objection is "a woman got it," which is the least defensible version of your complaint — and it's the one they'll be most prepared to rebut. If you ever do develop a genuine case, this framing is the thing their lawyers will quote back at you.

**The credential comparison is less lopsided than it looks**

I'd gently push back on the implicit reading that a PhD plus nine years of modelling obviously beats a master's plus regulatory experience. *Head* of risk modelling is substantially a management and stakeholder role. A large part of the job is owning the model risk framework, surviving supervisory review, getting internal models approved, and defending methodology choices to regulators who are not statisticians. "Broad experience of regulatory affairs" is a real qualification for that, not a euphemism. Your profile might have read as an outstanding individual contributor; hers might have read as someone who can carry the regulator relationship and the committee politics. You also can't see how either of you performed in the interviews, which for a leadership hire is often decisive.

That doesn't mean they got it right. It means the decision has a plausible innocent explanation, which matters for how you proceed.

**What's actually worth pursuing**

The real grievance here is the two weeks of silence. That's a process failure and it's concrete. I'd send a short, neutral follow-up: reference your original request by date, ask for the panel's assessment against the published criteria, and ask who the appropriate contact is if they can't provide it. Keep the tone of someone gathering feedback for future applications, because that's the framing most likely to get an actual answer.

Depending on where you are, you may have stronger tools. In the UK or EU, a data subject access request will typically get you interview notes and scoring sheets that mention you, and it's a legal obligation with a deadline rather than a favour. That's a far more productive lever than speculation about the panel. If you tell me the jurisdiction I can be more specific.

**What would actually be a signal**

Worth watching for: scoring criteria that appear to have been written or reweighted after the interviews; a job spec that emphasised technical depth being retrospectively described as a stakeholder role; any record of diversity targets tied to this specific appointment; a pattern across multiple senior hires rather than a single instance. Those are the things that make a case. The gender count on a four-person panel is not.
